addressed_problems.content: The current strategy for discovering winning tickets at initialization via layer pruning relies on a one-shot (non-iterative) importance estimation using criteria such as GraSP. Iterative pruning schemes, which alternate pruning and retraining, have been shown to produce more effective subnetworks in other pruning contexts. Developing an iterative layer-pruning method that can operate at initialization—thereby retaining the computational benefits of pruning before training while achieving the superior accuracy of iterative schedules—remains an open problem.

The layer-pruning formulation of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) is theoretically and technically confined to residual-like architectures (e.g., ResNets) because identity-mapping shortcuts are essential to allow layer removal without catastrophic representation collapse. Plain (non-residual) networks such as VGG lack these shortcuts, making layer pruning infeasible for them. Extending layer-pruning LTH to non-residual topologies—for instance, by designing alternative mechanisms that preserve information flow after layer removal—is an unresolved challenge.

Although most layer-pruned tickets at initialization are winning tickets, in 5 out of 14 reported configurations the subnetworks underperformed their dense counterparts by small margins. No clear pattern has emerged to explain these failures: potential factors include interactions with network depth, the specific location of pruned layers, dataset statistics, or optimization dynamics. Understanding the root causes of these rare underperformance cases is an open issue that requires systematic investigation.

Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of layer-pruned initialization tickets exhibited inconsistent behavior across architectures: on ResNet32, OOD accuracy declined at higher pruning severities, whereas on ResNet56 it generally improved. Determining when and why layer-pruned tickets obtained at initialization generalize to distribution shifts—and what architectural or pruning factors govern this behavior—remains an unresolved question for future work.

The empirical results raise a conceptual question about the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: to what extent does the choice of the eliminated structure (weights, filters, or layers) fundamentally determine the emergence and properties of winning tickets, as well as their recoverability at initialization? While layer-pruned tickets easily become winning tickets at initialization, filter-pruned tickets do not, suggesting that the pruned structure plays a critical role. Characterizing this role theoretically and across diverse architectures, datasets, and pruning schedules is an open direction for research.

The work addresses whether the central empirical phenomenon of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) — that a dense neural network $\mathcal{F}$ contains sparse subnetworks $\mathcal{F}'$ (winning tickets) that, when trained from an inherited initialization $\theta_i$, recover the predictive ability of $\mathcal{F}$ (formalized as $Accuracy(\mathcal{F}') + \xi \geq Accuracy(\mathcal{F})$) — continues to hold when the pruning operation removes whole layers instead of weights or filters, and whether such layer-based winning tickets can be discovered before any training (pruning at initialization). Prior LTH and pruning-at-initialization work focused on removing individual weights (unstructured pruning) or filters/neurons (structured pruning). Those approaches have two practical limitations: (i) unstructured pruning often requires specialized sparse-computation frameworks or hardware to realize runtime benefits, and (ii) structured/filter pruning still operates on small elements (filters) and its efficacy at initialization and on shallow architectures has been questioned in prior studies. Moreover, most demonstrations of winning tickets rely on training a full over-parameterized dense network to completion to obtain weight trajectories $(\theta_i)$ used for weight-rewinding; this training requirement imposes high computational cost and energy consumption, preventing low-resource or green-AI adoption. Separately, prior layer-pruning work (outside the LTH literature) has shown that residual architectures can tolerate removed layers because identity shortcuts permit alternate information paths, suggesting potential runtime and latency gains if entire layers can be removed — but it is unknown whether the LTH phenomenon and pruning-at-initialization are valid when the pruned structure is whole layers. This gap prevents answering whether one can (a) obtain hardware-agnostic, latency-reducing winning tickets via layer removal, and (b) discover them without first training the dense network, which would enable substantial reductions in FLOPs, memory, training time and carbon emission while preserving or improving accuracy and robustness.

nodes.content: In the setting of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, researchers have mainly established the existence of winning tickets by pruning weights or filters and then retraining subnetworks from an inherited initialization $\theta_i$. Those results leave open whether whole-layer removal — a structured pruning operation that eliminates sequential computation and can reduce latency and memory in standard deep-learning frameworks — preserves the LTH property. Prior layer-pruning work showed residual networks tolerate removed layers due to identity shortcuts, but those studies did not examine whether the resulting permanently shallower networks can be rewound and trained to match the original dense accuracy; consequently, it remained unknown whether layer removal yields subnetworks that are true "winning tickets" under the usual LTH definition. Resolving this is important because, if true, layer-based tickets would be a more hardware-agnostic and latency-reducing form of sparsity than weight-level tickets, and would motivate new approaches for efficient training and deployment without specialized sparse-hardware support.

Prior pruning-at-initialization research targeted weight-level pruning and encountered mixed results: many initialization-only importance criteria underperform compared to pruning after training, and some works reported that initialization pruning was not better than random at high sparsities. Practitioners lacked a reliable, data-driven criterion tailored to structured, layer-wise pruning at initialization that would (a) operate without training the dense network, (b) produce hardware-amenable reductions in sequential computation (latency) by removing whole layers, and (c) succeed across shallow and deeper residual networks. The absence of such an initialization method prevented replacing dense-network training with direct training of a shallower network obtained before any training, which would otherwise reduce FLOPs, memory and energy costs.

Designing an importance criterion that estimates which entire layers can be removed at initialization is challenging because untrained weights change drastically during early training, making many static or magnitude-based scores unreliable. SNIP and many other proposed initialization schemes were developed for weight-level pruning and may not translate to coarse, layer-level removals; without a criterion that preserves the network's representational capacity when layers are removed, initialization pruning can produce severely damaged subnetworks that cannot recover during subsequent training. A criterion robust to these issues is required to discover hardware-amenable, layer-pruned tickets at $\theta_0$.

Structured LTH studies commonly focus on filter/neuron removal as the structured pruning operation. Yet filter pruning at initialization has exhibited weak performance in prior work and in the authors' experiments, especially in shallow networks. Because filters are smaller-granularity structures than layers, it is unclear whether filter-level initialization pruning can preserve the representational pathways that residual modules provide, or whether removing coarser building blocks (layers) would be more suitable for initialization-based discovery of winning tickets. A direct empirical comparison with matched retained-filter counts was necessary to determine which structured removal yields superior initialization-pruning outcomes and whether filter-based structured LTH is fundamentally limited compared to layer-removal.

The dominant approach to obtain winning tickets has required training an over-parameterized dense network to completion in order to locate subnetworks by pruning; this imposes significant compute, energy and CO₂ costs. While weight-level or filter-level pruning can reduce parameter counts, their practical runtime and latency benefits are often limited without specialized sparse-computation hardware. Removing entire layers is a hardware-agnostic operation that reduces sequential computation and memory usage in standard frameworks, but prior to this work it was unknown whether layer-pruned subnetworks discovered at initialization could match the dense network accuracy; without that guarantee, one could not safely substitute and train a shallower network to obtain the claimed resource savings. Demonstrating initialization-discovered layer tickets that are winning tickets therefore addresses the practical barrier to green, low-cost training.

Prior work has found that pruning can increase adversarial robustness and OOD generalization in some settings, but most evidence focused on weight or filter pruning and/or pruning after or during training. It was unclear whether hardware-amenable, layer-pruned subnetworks discovered at initialization would preserve, improve, or degrade robustness and OOD performance after training with standard procedures. Understanding robustness behavior is critical for safety-sensitive applications and for assessing whether the computational gains of layer pruning come at the expense of reliability under distribution shift or adversarial perturbations.

In LTH studies, the choice of rewind epoch $\theta_i$ (the point in the dense-network training trajectory to which retained weights are reset) is known to affect whether a pruned subnetwork can recover accuracy. Prior LTH work observed that rewinding to early epochs often helps recovery, yet those studies principally considered weight- or filter-level pruning. For layer pruning, it was unknown how the rewind epoch interacts with the coarser structural damage caused by removing entire layers: if rewinding too late, the subnetwork may not have sufficient remaining training epochs to compensate for removed layers; if rewinding to initialization or early epochs, the subnetwork may recover better. Establishing this behavior is necessary to know whether layer-pruned tickets require different rewinding practices than other pruning granularities.

Several LTH and early-bird-ticket studies found that the important parameters or subnetworks that ultimately succeed are identifiable early in training, enabling earlier extraction and reduced dense-network training. However, those findings concentrated on weight- or filter-level pruning. For layer-pruned subnetworks to be practical, it is necessary to know whether they too exhibit early emergence so that one can design rewinding heuristics or early stopping rules; absent this knowledge, practitioners would need to complete dense training to locate successful layer removals, negating initialization or early-extraction benefits.

Removing entire residual blocks (layers) from a trained ResNet32 convolutional residual network on CIFAR-10 can produce subnetworks $\mathcal{F}'$ that satisfy the winning-ticket criterion $Accuracy(\mathcal{F}') + \xi \geq Accuracy(\mathcal{F})$ (with tolerance $\xi$ commonly one percentage point), i.e., layer-pruned subnetworks can match or exceed the accuracy of their dense counterparts. This behavior was observed empirically across multiple layer-importance criteria (HRank, expectABS, PLS, KL, Random) and multiple rewind epochs $\theta_i$, demonstrating that whole-layer removal yields valid winning tickets under the standard Lottery Ticket Hypothesis experimental protocol of training a dense network, pruning layers, rewinding to an earlier epoch, and retraining.

metadata.narrative: P1 limits the architectural scope of the existence claim to ResNet32, leaving generalizability to other residual networks unsubstantiated. H1 partially compensates by showing the effect is robust across multiple pruning criteria on that architecture, validating the existence at the mechanism level for the tested case. The overall prior probability reflects a well-supported but narrowly scoped conclusion.

nodes.title: Existence of winning tickets when pruning removes entire layers

nodes.content: It is possible to discover layer-pruned winning tickets before any training (pruning at initialization) by applying the GraSP importance criterion to randomly initialized residual networks. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet32, GraSP-derived layer-pruned subnetworks at random initialization $\theta_0$ matched or outperformed the dense baseline across pruning densities $p=1\ldots5$ (reported improvements include (+)0.40 at $p=1$, (+)0.72 at $p=2$, (+)0.34 at $p=3$, (+)0.41 at $p=4$, (+)0.12 at $p=5$ in percentage points relative to the dense model), demonstrating that GraSP can reliably identify layer-removal masks at $\theta_0$ that produce winning tickets after standard training of the pruned architecture.

metadata.narrative: P2 casts uncertainty on the quantitative reliability of the GraSP improvements, as the reported differences may be within run-to-run noise. H2 provides qualitative support through CKA similarity analysis, suggesting that GraSP indeed preserves representational structure even if the exact accuracy margins are uncertain. The conclusion is directionally plausible but quantitatively unvalidated.

nodes.title: Winning tickets from layer removal can be discovered at initialization using GraSP

nodes.content: The SNIP initialization criterion, when used to rank whole layers at random initialization, fails to produce winning layer-pruned tickets at higher pruning densities: on ResNet32, SNIP-derived layer-pruned subnetworks cease to be winning tickets beyond removing two residual blocks (reported declines of (-)0.50, (-)0.53, (-)1.00 percentage points at pruning densities $p=3,4,5$). In contrast, GraSP-derived layer-pruned subnetworks remained winning tickets across all tested densities up to $p=5$. Thus, GraSP is empirically more robust than SNIP for layer-pruning at initialization.

metadata.narrative: P3 introduces the same statistical concern for the comparison between SNIP and GraSP. H3's monotonic decline pattern for SNIP reduces the likelihood that the observed ineffectiveness is noise, lending confidence to the qualitative direction. The cross-density pattern is more robust than individual points, but the conclusion remains partially supported.

nodes.title: SNIP is ineffective for highly layer-sparse initial pruning while GraSP remains effective

nodes.content: When comparing structured pruning modalities at initialization with matched filter counts, layer-pruned subnetworks (whole-layer removal) discovered at initialization outperform filter-pruned subnetworks produced at initialization. On ResNet32, in the one-layer-removed setting (pruning density $p=1$), layer pruning yielded improvements of (+)0.08 and (+)0.40 percentage points using SNIP and GraSP respectively, whereas filter-pruning at initialization produced declines of (-)0.79 and (-)0.11 percentage points respectively. This indicates that, at initialization, removing entire layers is a more effective structured pruning strategy than removing an approximately equivalent number of filters.

metadata.narrative: P4 severely limits the generality of the comparison to a single density and architecture. H4 ensures the comparison is fair at that density, but the conclusion's broad claim of superiority cannot be trusted beyond the tested regime. The prior probability is low due to the narrow evidence base.

nodes.title: Layer-pruned tickets at initialization outperform filter-pruned (structured) LTH tickets at initialization

nodes.content: Layer-pruned winning tickets found at initialization yield concrete runtime and resource benefits when trained in place of the dense network: reported improvements include reductions in FLOPs up to 45.00%, memory consumption reductions up to 45.82%, CO₂ emission reductions up to 51.11%, and training time speedups up to $2.03\times$ (ResNet56, pruning density $p=12$). Smaller pruning densities also produced notable savings (e.g., ResNet32, $p=4$: FLOPs -34.13%, memory -30.11%, CO₂ -33.33%, training speedup $1.57\times$). These gains arise because entire layers are removed prior to training, enabling training of a permanently shallower network with no prior dense-network training cost.

metadata.narrative: P5 weakens the quantitative precision of the CO₂ savings, but H5 provides a comprehensive multi-metric characterization that confirms the direction of substantial savings. The conclusion is strongly supported for FLOPs, memory, and time; the environmental component requires more careful validation.

nodes.title: Layer-pruned winning tickets discovered at initialization provide substantial computational and environmental savings

nodes.content: Layer-pruned winning tickets found at initialization and trained with standard (clean) CIFAR-10 training often exhibit improved robustness to common corruptions and improved out-of-distribution generalization: on CIFAR-C the reported improvements over dense models reach up to (+)3.73 percentage points (ResNet56, pruning density $p=4$), while on CIFAR-10.2 the reported improvements reach up to (+)1.75 percentage points (ResNet56, $p=4$). Some configurations underperform the dense baseline (5 of 14 reported), but many layer-pruned initialization tickets increased robustness and out-of-distribution accuracy relative to their dense counterparts.

metadata.narrative: P6 casts doubt on the statistical reliability of the robustness improvements. H6 broadens the evidence base by including two separate OOD datasets. The qualitative finding that layer-pruned tickets can improve robustness is partially supported, but the overall conclusion is hampered by the lack of replication.

nodes.title: Layer-pruned winning tickets discovered at initialization improve robustness and sometimes OOD generalization

nodes.content: When extracting layer-pruned subnetworks from a trained dense network and rewinding their weights to an earlier epoch $\theta_i$ (where $i$ indicates the training epoch), rewinding to the original initialization $\theta_0$ or to early epochs generally enables layer-pruned subnetworks to become winning tickets, whereas rewinding to later epochs can reduce recovery accuracy. Empirically on ResNet32, subnetworks rewound to $\theta_0$ were winning tickets across most pruning criteria (e.g., KL: (+)0.74 percentage points at $\theta_0$), and many criteria attained top accuracy when rewound to early epochs rather than mid/late epochs; subnetworks rewound after 50 epochs showed lower accuracy in several cases.

metadata.narrative: P7 limits the rewinding benefit evidence to ResNet32. H7 shows the early-rewinding pattern is robust across multiple criteria on that architecture. The conclusion is well-supported for ResNet32 but its general scope is unverified.

nodes.title: Weight rewinding and early-epoch inheritance promote layer-pruned winning tickets

nodes.content: Layer-pruned subnetworks share the structured-LTH property of emerging early: the best-practice rewinding epochs for layer-pruned subnetworks are early in the dense-network training trajectory, consistent with the notion that subnetworks that will become winning tickets stabilize their important parameters early in training. This early-emergence property holds across multiple pruning criteria and informs practical rules for weight rewinding and early-bird detection when layers are the pruned structure.

metadata.narrative: P8 limits the early-emergence evidence to ResNet32. H8 provides cross-criteria consistency on that architecture, supporting the claim qualitatively. As with C7, the generalization to deeper networks remains unvalidated.

nodes.title: Layer-pruned subnetworks emerge early in training similarly to structured LTH tickets

nodes.content: Layer-pruned winning tickets achieved via weight rewinding have been demonstrated exclusively on the ResNet32 architecture trained on CIFAR-10, with no experiments on other convolutional residual architectures such as ResNet56, ResNet110, or WideResNet.Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If the undisclosed architectures (e.g., ResNet56) do not exhibit winning tickets under the same weight-rewinding protocol — for instance, if removing a single layer from a deeper network irreparably damages its representational capacity — then the conclusion that "removing entire residual blocks from a trained convolutional residual network can produce subnetworks that satisfy the winning-ticket criterion" would be false for those architectures. The claim's scope would be limited to ResNet32, contradicting the general phrasing of the conclusion.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's Conclusion 1 is stated for "convolutional residual network" generally, yet the supporting experiment (Table 1) uses a single architecture (ResNet32). Prior work (Liu et al., 2022) indicates that pruning-at-initialization behavior can differ markedly between shallow and deep networks; the weight-rewinding behavior for layer pruning might similarly vary with depth. Without evidence from at least one additional architecture (e.g., ResNet56, which the paper itself uses for other experiments), the claim of general existence across all convolutional residual networks lacks empirical grounding.

nodes.title: Layer-pruned winning tickets from weight rewinding tested only on ResNet32 on CIFAR-10

nodes.content: In experiments on CIFAR-10 with ResNet32, the accuracy improvements of GraSP-derived layer-pruned subnetworks at initialization are reported as single-point values (e.g., (+)0.12 percentage points at pruning density $p=5$) without variance estimates such as standard deviation, multiple seeds, or confidence intervals. This prevents assessment of whether the positive differences are statistically distinguishable from zero or from the run-to-run variability of the dense baseline model.Table 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the true population accuracy difference between the GraSP-layer-pruned subnetwork and the dense model is close to zero or slightly negative (i.e., the observed positive differences are artifacts of a single run), then the core claim of Conclusion 2 — that GraSP discovers winning tickets at initialization with improvements over the dense baseline — collapses. The reported improvements would not be reproducible, and the practical recommendation to use GraSP for layer pruning at initialization would lack statistical support.
metadata.weakness_reason: In deep learning training on CIFAR-10, run-to-run accuracy can easily vary by multiple tenths of a percentage point due to stochastic initialization, data shuffling, and batch order. The improvements in Table 2 are tiny (0.12–0.72 pp); without replication, one cannot rule out that these values arise from noise. The paper neither states the number of trials nor provides error bars, which is a standard requirement for conclusions that depend on small numerical differences.

nodes.title: Accuracy improvements of GraSP at initialization reported without variance estimates

nodes.content: In experiments comparing SNIP and GraSP for layer pruning at initialization on CIFAR-10 with ResNet32, the accuracy differences that indicate SNIP is ineffective (negative at pruning densities $p=3,4,5$) and GraSP is effective (positive at all $p$) are reported without variance estimates. Therefore, it is unknown whether these differences are statistically reliable or due to noise from a single run per condition.Table 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the performance gap between SNIP and GraSP is actually smaller or reversed upon replication — for instance, if SNIP's decline at p=3 is within the noise and GraSP's advantage is not robust — then Conclusion 3's strong claim that "SNIP fails to produce winning tickets at higher densities while GraSP remains effective" would be unsupported. The practical guidance to prefer GraSP over SNIP for layer pruning would be empirically unfounded.
metadata.weakness_reason: Same as P2. The magnitudes of the differences (e.g., -0.50 pp for SNIP at p=3 vs +0.34 pp for GraSP at p=3) are within a range that could be produced by inter-run variation. Without multiple seeds or error bars, the reliability of the comparison is uncertain, especially for the borderline cases (p=3: -0.50 vs +0.34).

nodes.title: SNIP and GraSP accuracy differences at initialization reported without variance estimates

nodes.content: The comparison between layer pruning and filter pruning at initialization, with matched filter counts, has been performed only at pruning density $p=1$ (one layer removed) on CIFAR-10 with ResNet32. No results are reported for higher pruning densities ($p=2,3,4,5$) or on other architectures.Table 3

metadata.failure_mode: If at higher densities (e.g., p=3 or p=5) filter pruning at initialization matches or exceeds layer pruning, then the conclusion that "layer-pruned tickets at initialization outperform filter-pruned tickets at initialization" would be false for those regimes. The general claim would need to be revised to apply only to low-density pruning, which would significantly reduce its practical impact since larger savings come at higher densities.
metadata.weakness_reason: The claim in C4 is phrased as a general superiority of layer pruning over filter pruning at initialization. However, the experiment only examines the lowest possible sparsity regime. Filter pruning performance relative to layer pruning might change at higher pruning densities: removing many filters could be less damaging than removing multiple entire layers, which removes all filters in a block. Without testing at higher densities, the generality of the superiority claim is unsupported.

nodes.title: Layer vs filter pruning at initialization compared only at pruning density p=1

nodes.content: CO₂ emission reductions (up to 51.11%) for layer-pruned winning tickets at initialization are estimated using a formula from Lacoste et al. (2019), but the specific hardware (GPU model, power draw), runtime measurement method, and training hyperparameters for the dense and subnetwork runs are not reported. No direct power measurements or validation against actual energy meters are provided.Table 4

metadata.failure_mode: If the actual CO₂ savings under a more detailed measurement are substantially lower (e.g., due to lower GPU utilization or energy overhead not captured), the quantitative claim of up to 51.11% CO₂ reduction would be inaccurate. The conclusion's statement that "CO₂ emission reductions up to 51.11%" is a key selling point for green AI; if overestimated, it could mislead policy and practice, and the general claim of "substantial computational and environmental savings" would lose its environmental leg.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper provides a citation to Lacoste et al. but does not detail the inputs to the formula (runtime, GPU utilization, power consumption). Different GPU models and system configurations can produce widely different CO₂ estimates for the same training task. Without this information, the reported percentages cannot be independently verified or meaningfully compared across studies. The FLOPs and memory savings are deterministic, but the CO₂ metric is sensitive to assumptions.

nodes.title: CO₂ emission reductions estimated without specified hardware, measurement method, or validation

nodes.content: Robustness improvements of layer-pruned winning tickets at initialization on CIFAR-C and CIFAR-10.2 are reported as single-point differences without variance estimates or multiple-seed replication. Consequently, it is unknown whether observed improvements such as (+)3.73 percentage points on CIFAR-C for ResNet56 at pruning density $p=4$ are statistically reliable or could be due to run-to-run variability in clean CIFAR-10 training.Table 5

metadata.failure_mode: If the robustness improvements are not reproducible (i.e., the observed positive differences are within the noise of a particular run), then the claim that layer-pruned tickets "often exhibit improved robustness" would be unsupported. The conclusion's practical implication for safety-critical applications would be unreliable, as the observed improvements might not persist in deployment.
metadata.weakness_reason: Same as P2. The dense baseline model used for comparison is itself a single run. Robustness evaluation on fixed corruption sets introduces little stochasticity, but the base model's accuracy varies across runs; therefore, the difference between subnetwork and dense baseline could shift sign if re-run with a different seed. Without replication, one cannot trust that the improvements are systematic rather than noise.

nodes.title: Robustness improvements of layer-pruned tickets reported without variance estimates

nodes.content: Experimental support for weight rewinding to $\theta_0$ or early epochs promoting layer-pruned winning tickets is based exclusively on ResNet32 on CIFAR-10. No analogous experiments on other residual architectures (e.g., ResNet56) have been conducted, leaving the generalizability across network depths unexamined.Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If for deeper architectures like ResNet56 the optimal rewind epoch is later or rewinding to early epochs is no better than random initialization, then Conclusion 7's general recommendation would be valid only for ResNet32. The practical advice to practitioners using deeper residual networks would be misleading, as the benefit might not materialize in their setting.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper extensively uses ResNet56 for initialization and robustness experiments, yet does not report weight-rewinding results for that or any other architecture. Prior LTH literature shows that optimal rewind epochs can depend on network size and depth. Without testing on a deeper model, the claim that "rewinding to the original initialization θ0 or to early epochs generally enables layer-pruned subnetworks to become winning tickets" is founded on a single datapoint.

nodes.title: Weight rewinding benefit for layer-pruned tickets tested only on ResNet32 on CIFAR-10

nodes.content: The evidence that the best rewind epochs for layer-pruned subnetworks are early in training comes solely from experiments on ResNet32 on CIFAR-10, with no support from other residual architectures. The generality of this early-emergence property across different network depths and widths is therefore unknown.Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If deeper residual networks do not exhibit early emergence (i.e., their best rewind epoch is not at θ0 or early), then Conclusion 8's claim that "layer-pruned subnetworks share the structured-LTH property of emerging early" would not hold for those architectures, limiting its scope and contradicting the general phrasing.
metadata.weakness_reason: Same as P7. The claim is about a property of "layer-pruned subnetworks" generally, but the evidence base is a single architecture. The early-emergence property might be architecture-dependent; deeper networks might have a longer critical window or a different stability period for parameters.

nodes.title: Early-emergence property of layer-pruned tickets tested only on ResNet32 on CIFAR-10

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet32, when layer pruning is applied to a trained network and weights are rewound to θ0, five pruning criteria (HRank, expectABS, PLS, Random, KL) all produce subnetworks that satisfy the winning-ticket condition Accuracy(F') + ξ ≥ Accuracy(F), with four criteria showing positive accuracy improvements and the fifth showing a negligible decline of 0.01 percentage points (Table 1).

metadata.credit: This convergence across five structurally diverse importance functions (rank-based, expected-magnitude-based, projection-based, divergence-based, and random) preempts the failure mode where the observed winning tickets could be an artifact of a single criterion's peculiar interaction with training dynamics. The pattern substantiates the qualitative existence of layer-pruned winning tickets (C1) as a robust phenomenon independent of the specific metric used to score layer importance, underwritten at the mechanism layer by the consistency of the outcome across different signal-extraction methods.

nodes.title: Multiple pruning criteria confirm winning tickets

nodes.content: For GraSP-derived layer-pruned subnetworks on CIFAR-10 with ResNet32 across pruning densities p=1 to p=5, the Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity between the subnetwork's internal representations and the original dense network's representations decreased only slightly with pruning severity, while for SNIP-derived subnetworks the CKA similarity dropped markedly (e.g., nearly two percentage points at p=5).

metadata.credit: The CKA analysis provides an independent, convergent line of evidence that GraSP preserves the representational structure of the dense network, addressing the failure mode where small positive accuracy differences alone might be noise. Even if the accuracy improvements are not statistically robust, the representational similarity check suggests that GraSP indeed selects layers whose removal least distorts the network's internal computation, lending qualitative support to the mechanism underlying C2. The scope of credit is limited to the qualitative direction; the precision of the accuracy advantage remains uncertain.

nodes.title: CKA similarity supports GraSP's effectiveness

nodes.content: For SNIP-based layer-pruning at initialization on CIFAR-10 with ResNet32, the accuracy difference relative to the dense network decreases monotonically with pruning density: (+)0.08 at p=1, (+)0.00 at p=2, (-)0.50 at p=3, (-)0.53 at p=4, (-)1.00 at p=5 percentage points (Table 2).

metadata.credit: The strictly decreasing sequence across five independently measured density levels is a pattern unlikely to arise from independent noise, preempting the failure mode that the observed decline at individual densities could be random fluctuations. This pattern provides qualitative support for the claim that SNIP becomes ineffective as the number of layers removed increases (C3). The monotonic trend underwrites the directionality of the claim, though the precise quantitative thresholds remain uncertain due to the lack of error bars.

nodes.title: Monotonic decline of SNIP accuracy supports ineffectiveness at high density

nodes.content: When comparing layer pruning and filter pruning at initialization on CIFAR-10 with ResNet32 at pruning density p=1, the number of remaining filters in the subnetwork was matched: after removing one layer (1200 filters remaining), filter pruning was forced to remove the closest possible number of filters to achieve the same total filter count as the layer-pruned subnetwork (Table 3 description).

metadata.credit: This matching procedure preempts the failure mode that the apparent superiority of layer pruning could be an artifact of the layer-pruned subnetwork retaining more parameters (filters) than the filter-pruned one. By equalizing the filter count, the comparison isolates the type of structure removed from the confounding factor of capacity, strengthening C4's claim that layer pruning is a more effective structured pruning strategy at initialization, at least for the tested low-density regime.

nodes.title: Matched filter count controls for model capacity

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet32 (pruning densities p=1,3,4) and ResNet56 (p=3,4,5,12), layer-pruned winning tickets at initialization yield simultaneous reductions in FLOPs (up to 45.00%), memory consumption (up to 45.82%), CO₂ emission (up to 51.11%), and training time speedup (up to 2.03×), as reported in Table 4 across fourteen metric-architecture-density combinations.

metadata.credit: The inclusion of four complementary performance metrics across two architectures and multiple densities provides a multi-faceted assessment of the practical benefits, guarding against the failure mode where a single metric (e.g., FLOPs) might not translate to real-world savings (e.g., wall-clock time or environmental impact). The consistent positive direction across all fourteen reported configurations underwrites the qualitative and quantitative direction of C5's claim about substantial savings, although the exact numerical percentages for CO₂ remain less precisely supported than the deterministic metrics.

nodes.title: Comprehensive multi-metric savings characterization

nodes.content: For layer-pruned winning tickets at initialization on CIFAR-10 with ResNet32 and ResNet56, robustness was evaluated on two distinct out-of-distribution datasets: CIFAR-C (fifteen common corruptions) and CIFAR-10.2 (natural distribution shift), covering both synthetic corruptions and real-world domain shift (Table 5).

metadata.credit: The use of two separate OOD evaluation benchmarks with different sources of distribution shift preempts the failure mode that observed robustness improvements on one corruption set might be artifacts of that specific transformation set, thereby broadening the evidence base for C6. The partial but substantial set of positive results across both datasets (9 of 14 configurations improve) supports the qualitative finding that layer-pruned tickets can improve robustness, though the inconsistency (5 underperformed) prevents strong quantitative conclusions.

nodes.title: Evaluation on two OOD datasets broadens robustness evidence

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet32, across five pruning criteria (HRank, expectABS, PLS, Random, KL), rewinding layer-pruned subnetworks to the original initialization θ0 or to an early epoch (θ25) consistently yields higher or comparable accuracy compared to rewinding to later epochs (θ50, θ75), with four of five criteria showing positive improvements at θ0 and most criteria showing declines at θ75 (Table 1).

metadata.credit: This consistency across five structurally different importance functions preempts the failure mode where a particular criterion's interaction with rewinding dynamics could produce a spurious early-epoch advantage. The pattern substantiates the qualitative direction of C7 — that early rewinding promotes layer-pruned winning tickets — as a phenomenon intrinsic to layer-pruning LTH rather than a criterion-specific artifact.

nodes.title: Consistent early-rewinding benefit across multiple criteria

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet32, the weight-rewinding experiment (Table 1) shows that for five pruning criteria, the best-practice rewind epoch is early (θ0 or θ25) rather than mid/late (θ50 or θ75), indicating that layer-pruned subnetworks that will become winning tickets stabilize their important parameters early in training.

metadata.credit: This convergence across multiple criteria preempts the failure mode that the early-emergence property could be an artifact of a single importance measure. The pattern supports C8's claim that layer-pruned subnetworks share the structured-LTH property of emerging early despite the coarser granularity of removal, reinforcing the analogy between filter-level and layer-level LTH at the mechanism layer.

nodes.title: Consistent pattern of best rewind epoch being early across criteria

steps.reasoning: State the formal winning-ticket criterion used by the authors: denote the dense network as $\mathcal{F}$ and a pruned subnetwork as $\mathcal{F}'$; a winning ticket is defined as any $\mathcal{F}'$ that satisfies $Accuracy(\mathcal{F}') + \xi \geq Accuracy(\mathcal{F})$, where $\xi \geq 0$ is a tolerance parameter (commonly one percentage point or one standard deviation in practice).

Summarize the layer-pruning LTH procedure the authors use to test the existence of winning tickets when removing layers: train the dense network $\mathcal{F}$ to completion to obtain $\theta_n$, compute layer importance scores $S$ using a chosen pruning criterion $c$, remove the $p$ least important layers to obtain $\mathcal{F}'$, set $\mathcal{F}'$'s weights to a rewind epoch $\theta_i$ (this can be $\theta_0$ or some early epoch), then train $\mathcal{F}'$ for the remaining epochs and compare its accuracy to the dense baseline via the above criterion. This procedure is summarized in the authors' Algorithm 1.

Invoke the upstream result that weight rewinding to early epochs (including $\theta_0$) promotes layer-pruned subnetworks becoming winning tickets: take as established that rewinding to $\theta_0$ or an early $\theta_i$ generally enables recovery to winning-ticket accuracy (this upstream result is the conclusion that weight rewinding and early-epoch inheritance promote layer-pruned winning tickets).

Describe the experimental evidence the authors provide for layer removal producing winning tickets: in the ResNet32 experiments on CIFAR-10 across multiple layer-importance criteria (HRank, expectABS, PLS, KL, Random) and multiple rewind epochs $\theta_i$, the authors report that rewinding to $\theta_0$ enabled all subnetworks to become winning tickets except HRank which showed a negligible drop (Table 1); in particular, several criteria show positive accuracy differences when rewound to early epochs (e.g., expectABS (+)0.33 at $\theta_0$, KL (+)0.74 at $\theta_0$), demonstrating that subnetworks produced by removing whole residual blocks match or exceed the accuracy of the dense network under the standard LTH experimental protocol. 
Table 1

Note the authors' aggregate statement and conclusion based on these experiments: "Altogether, the previous results confirm the existence of winning tickets when the pruning process removes entire layers," thereby answering the paper's first research question affirmatively that layer-pruned subnetworks $\mathcal{F}'$ can satisfy $Accuracy(\mathcal{F}') + \xi \geq Accuracy(\mathcal{F})$ using common tolerances $\xi$ on the order of a percentage point.

Record the scope and conditions the authors specify for this claim: the empirical observation is demonstrated on CIFAR-10 using residual architectures (ResNet32 and similar architectures), across multiple layer-importance criteria (HRank, expectABS, PLS, KL, Random) and multiple rewind epochs $\theta_i$, and follows the standard experimental LTH protocol where the pruned network is trained after rewinding; the authors also note practical constraints (e.g., the method applies to residual-like networks and cannot be applied to plain VGG-like networks due to technical incompatibilities). 
Table 1
Algorithm 1

Treat as established the upstream results: (a) layer-pruned winning tickets exist (the conclusion that removing entire residual blocks can produce winning tickets), and (b) SNIP is ineffective at high layer sparsities while GraSP remains effective at initialization (the conclusion that GraSP is empirically more robust than SNIP). These upstream conclusions are taken as given for the present derivation.

Define the pruning-at-initialization procedure used to discover tickets before any training: starting from an untrained convolutional network $\mathcal{F}$ at random initialization $\theta_0$, compute layer importance scores $S$ with an initialization criterion $c$ (SNIP or GraSP), remove the $p$ least important layers to obtain $\mathcal{F}'$, and then train $\mathcal{F}'$ for the full training schedule to evaluate its final accuracy; this procedure is summarized in Algorithm 2. 
Algorithm 2

Report the initialization experiment results that support GraSP's ability to discover layer-pruned winning tickets at initialization: in the ResNet32 CIFAR-10 experiments the GraSP-derived layer-pruned subnetworks at initialization have accuracy differences relative to the dense baseline of (+)0.40 at $p=1$, (+)0.72 at $p=2$, (+)0.34 at $p=3$, (+)0.41 at $p=4$, and (+)0.12 at $p=5$, i.e., all positive differences for $p=1\ldots5$, indicating GraSP-selected layer-removal masks at $\theta_0$ produce subnetworks that match or exceed the dense model after training. 
Table 2

Explain the contrast with SNIP using the same table: SNIP's initialization-selected layer-pruned subnetworks show declines at higher pruning densities (negative differences at $p=3,4,5$), whereas GraSP maintains positive improvements across the tested $p$ values, which empirically demonstrates GraSP's reliability for identifying layer-removal masks at $\theta_0$ that lead to winning tickets after training the pruned architecture. 
Table 2

Record supporting analysis the authors provide beyond raw accuracy: the authors measure representation similarity (CKA) between the dense network and the subnetworks; they report that GraSP subnetworks retain internal representations closer to the dense network across pruning severities (CKA differences small even at high $p$), whereas SNIP subnetworks' representation similarity degrades with severity; this supports the empirical observation that GraSP-selected initialization masks more effectively preserve trainable structure that enables winning-ticket behavior. 
Kornblith et al. [2019]

State the empirical conclusion: thus, it is possible to discover layer-pruned winning tickets at initialization by applying GraSP to randomly initialized residual networks, and on CIFAR-10 with ResNet32 GraSP-derived layer-pruned subnetworks at initialization matched or outperformed the dense baseline across pruning densities $p=1\ldots5$ with the specific improvements reported above. 
Table 2

Define the pruning-at-initialization setting: pruning at initialization selects structures to remove using the random initialization of a network, denoted $\theta_{0}$, before any training takes place; here the pruning density $p$ denotes the number of residual blocks (layers) removed (e.g., $p=1$ removes one residual block).

Define the two initialization importance criteria considered: SNIP (where importance for a weight is computed as the product of the weight and its gradient at initialization, then the absolute value is taken) and GraSP (a variant of SNIP that considers the signal of the weight in importance estimation); both SNIP and GraSP use data and labels forwarded through the randomly initialized network to compute gradients and hence are data-driven. 
Lee et al. (2019)
Wang et al. (2020)

Describe the experimental protocol used to compare SNIP and GraSP at initialization: the authors apply each criterion to randomly initialized ResNet32 on the CIFAR-10 dataset, remove $p$ residual blocks according to the criterion's layer scores, construct the pruned network $\mathcal{F}'$ by physically removing those layers, and then train $\mathcal{F}'$ for the full training schedule; performance is reported as the difference in top-1 accuracy (in percentage points) between the pruned network $\mathcal{F}'$ and the dense network $\mathcal{F}$, where a positive value denotes a winning ticket according to the criterion $Accuracy(\mathcal{F}') + \xi \geq Accuracy(\mathcal{F})$ with small $\xi$ (one percentage point or one standard deviation commonly used). 
Table 2

Report the empirical results from the initialization experiment (ResNet32 on CIFAR-10) as given in the authors' table: for SNIP the accuracy differences relative to the dense baseline are (+)0.08 at $p=1$, (+)0.00 at $p=2$, (-)0.50 at $p=3$, (-)0.53 at $p=4$, and (-)1.00 at $p=5$; for GraSP the accuracy differences are (+)0.40 at $p=1$, (+)0.72 at $p=2$, (+)0.34 at $p=3$, (+)0.41 at $p=4$, and (+)0.12 at $p=5$. 
Table 2

From these reported values, conclude that SNIP-derived layer-pruned subnetworks cease to be winning tickets beyond removing two residual blocks because SNIP's reported accuracy differences become negative at $p=3,4,5$ (declines of (-)0.50, (-)0.53, (-)1.00 percentage points respectively), whereas GraSP-derived layer-pruned subnetworks remain winning tickets across all tested densities $p=1\ldots5$ because GraSP's reported accuracy differences remain positive for all those $p$ values. 
Table 2

Present additional empirical support the authors provide for GraSP's superiority over SNIP at high layer sparsities: the authors measure representation similarity (Centered Kernel Alignment, CKA) between subnetworks and the dense network and report that at low pruning severity ($p=1$ the CKA difference between GraSP and SNIP subnetworks and the dense network is under one percentage point, with GraSP obtaining higher similarity), while at large pruning severity ($p=5$) the SNIP subnetwork's internal representation similarity to the dense network decreases by almost two percentage points relative to GraSP; this pattern is presented as reinforcing the positive accuracy results for GraSP. 
Kornblith et al. [2019]

State the empirical conclusion: therefore, SNIP is ineffective for discovering highly layer-sparse (large $p$) winning tickets at initialization on ResNet32, while GraSP remains effective across the tested densities, making GraSP empirically more robust than SNIP for layer-pruning at initialization in the presented experiments. 
Table 2

Start from the upstream result that GraSP can find layer-pruned winning tickets at initialization (the conclusion that GraSP-discovered layer-pruned subnetworks at $\theta_0$ win the lottery across $p=1\ldots5$ is taken as given).

Describe the fairness procedure the authors use to compare layer pruning to filter (structured) pruning at initialization: for a given layer-pruned subnetwork the authors compute the number of remaining filters after removing layers and then produce a filter-pruned subnetwork that removes the closest possible number of filters so that the two pruned networks are comparable in terms of filter sparsity; this ensures the filter-pruned and layer-pruned subnetworks have nearly matched numbers of filters for a fair comparison.

Report the comparison experiment performed on ResNet32 at the lowest sparsity regime ($p=1$; one residual block removed) and the observed performance differences: according to the authors' table, in the $p=1$ setting SNIP-initialized filter-pruned subnetworks decline by (-)0.79 percentage points relative to the dense model while SNIP-initialized layer-pruned subnetworks improve by (+)0.08 pp; under GraSP the filter-pruned subnetwork declines by (-)0.11 pp while the layer-pruned subnetwork improves by (+)0.40 pp. 
Table 3

From these numerical comparisons, infer the authors' empirical conclusion: at initialization and under matched filter-count sparsity, removing entire layers (layer pruning) yields better-performing subnetworks than removing an approximately equivalent number of filters (structured filter pruning), as shown by the layer-pruned subnetworks' positive improvements versus the filter-pruned subnetworks' declines in the one-layer-removed setting for both SNIP and GraSP. 
Table 3

Record the authors' interpretive remarks that accompany these results: the authors observe that layer removal corresponds to removing all filters at a specific location and that despite being somewhat counter-intuitive, layer-pruned subnetworks retain internal representations more similar to the dense network (CKA similarity) and hence achieve higher accuracy than filter-pruned subnetworks in these initialization experiments; the authors therefore conclude that, at initialization, removing entire layers is a more effective structured pruning strategy than removing an approximately equivalent number of filters. 
Table 3

Take as established the upstream fact that GraSP can discover layer-pruned winning tickets at initialization (so that training can proceed on the permanently shallower pruned network $\mathcal{F}'$ instead of the dense network $\mathcal{F}$); this upstream result motivates measuring computational and environmental benefits.

Define the performance metrics reported by the authors: FLOPs denotes floating point operations required during training; "memory consumption" refers to peak memory used during training; "CO$_2$ emission" reports the authors' estimate of carbon emissions during training; "training speed up" denotes the multiplicative factor of reduced wall-clock training time when training the pruned network $\mathcal{F}'$ in place of the dense network $\mathcal{F}$.

Report the quantitative performance gains presented by the authors for winning tickets discovered at initialization (as given in their Table 4): for ResNet32 winning tickets the authors report (p=1) FLOPs -6.82%, memory -10.13%, CO$_2$ -11.11%, training speedup $1.10\times$; (p=3) FLOPs -20.47%, memory -25.29%, CO$_2$ -25.92%, speedup $1.35\times$; (p=4) FLOPs -34.13%, memory -30.11%, CO$_2$ -33.33%, speedup $1.57\times$. For ResNet56 winning tickets the authors report (p=3) FLOPs -11.25%, memory -15.15%, CO$_2$ -13.33%, speedup $1.16\times$; (p=4) FLOPs -15.00%, memory -19.42%, CO$_2$ -20.00%, speedup $1.24\times$; (p=5) FLOPs -18.76%, memory -23.69%, CO$_2$ -24.44%, speedup $1.34\times$; and (p=12) FLOPs -45.00%, memory -45.82%, CO$_2$ -51.11%, speedup $2.03\times$. 
Table 4

Highlight the concrete example the authors emphasize: the largest reported savings occur for ResNet56 at $p=12$, where FLOPs reduction is 45.00%, memory consumption reduction is 45.82%, CO$_2$ emission reduction is 51.11%, and training-time speedup is $2.03\times$, demonstrating substantial resource and runtime savings when training the pruned network discovered at initialization. 
Table 4

Explain the mechanism by which these savings arise according to the authors: because the pruning removes entire layers prior to any training, the resulting $\mathcal{F}'$ is permanently shallower and therefore requires fewer floating point operations and less memory during training and inference, and no expensive initial dense training is required to discover $\mathcal{F}'$, so the reported savings are realized without incurring a prior dense-network training cost.

State the authors' empirical conclusion: therefore, layer-pruned winning tickets found at initialization provide substantial computational and environmental savings when trained in place of the dense network, with the reported quantitative gains (FLOPs, memory, CO$_2$, and training speedup) exemplified above. 
Table 4

Treat as established the upstream result that GraSP can find layer-pruned winning tickets at initialization (so that pruned networks discovered at $\theta_0$ can be trained and evaluated for robustness and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization).

Define the robustness and OOD evaluation tasks the authors use: CIFAR-C is a dataset of common corruptions used to measure robustness to corruptions; CIFAR-10.2 is a held-out reproduction dataset used to measure out-of-distribution generalization; the authors evaluate pruned networks trained with standard clean CIFAR-10 training (no adversarial training) and report improvements in accuracy relative to the dense baseline in percentage points. 
Hendrycks and Dietterich [2019]
Lu et al. [2020]

Report the empirical robustness and OOD results the authors provide in their Table 5: for ResNet32 winning tickets at initialization the CIFAR-C improvements are (+)1.13 at $p=1$, (-)0.05 at $p=3$, (+)1.61 at $p=4$ with corresponding CIFAR-10.2 changes of (+)0.00, (-)1.15, and (-)0.65 respectively; for ResNet56 winning tickets the CIFAR-C improvements are (+)0.59 at $p=3$, (+)3.73 at $p=4$, (-)0.16 at $p=5$, and (+)1.98 at $p=12$, while the CIFAR-10.2 improvements include (+)0.70 at $p=3$, (+)1.75 at $p=4$, (+)0.70 at $p=5$, and (-)1.95 at $p=12$. 
Table 5

From these numerical values, extract the authors' highlighted findings: the maximum reported CIFAR-C improvement is (+)3.73 percentage points for ResNet56 at $p=4$, and the maximum reported CIFAR-10.2 improvement is (+)1.75 percentage points for ResNet56 at $p=4$; however, some configurations (5 out of 14 reported configurations) underperform their dense equivalents, indicating the behavior is not uniformly positive across all settings. 
Table 5

State the authors' interpretive conclusion: overall, layer-pruned winning tickets discovered at initialization and trained with standard (clean) CIFAR-10 training often exhibit improved robustness to common corruptions and improved out-of-distribution generalization relative to the dense model, as evidenced by the reported improvements on CIFAR-C and CIFAR-10.2, even though some configurations underperform; the authors present this as indicating that benefits of their winning tickets extend beyond computational savings to robustness and OOD performance. 
Table 5

Define weight rewinding: for a dense network $\mathcal{F}$, denote by $\theta_i$ the parameters at training epoch $i$, with $\theta_0$ the random initialization and $\theta_n$ the parameters after training to completion; weight rewinding assigns the weights of the pruned subnetwork $\mathcal{F}'$ to some earlier $\theta_i$ (possibly $\theta_0$) before continuing training of $\mathcal{F}'$ for $n-i$ epochs.

Describe the LTH layer-pruning procedure used in the experiments: train the dense network $\mathcal{F}$ for $n$ epochs to obtain $\theta_n$, compute an importance score $S$ for each layer using a pruning criterion $c$, select the $p$ least important layers, remove those layers to obtain $\mathcal{F}'$, set the weights of $\mathcal{F}'$ to a rewind point $\theta_i$, and then train $\mathcal{F}'$ for the remaining $n-i$ epochs (this is the algorithmic summary the authors provide).

Describe the experimental setup for the weight-rewinding study: experiments are performed on ResNet32 trained on CIFAR-10; multiple layer-importance criteria are evaluated (HRank, expectABS, PLS, KL, Random); for each criterion the authors create subnetworks by removing layers and then set $\mathcal{F}'$'s weights to various rewind epochs $\theta_i$ (specifically $\theta_0$, $\theta_{25}$, $\theta_{50}$, and $\theta_{75}$) and train the pruned network accordingly to completion. 
Table 1

Report the empirical results from the rewind experiment as given in the authors' table: for each criterion the authors list the accuracy difference (in percentage points) between the rewound-and-trained $\mathcal{F}'$ and the dense network $\mathcal{F}$ for rewinds to $\theta_0$, $\theta_{25}$, $\theta_{50}$, and $\theta_{75}$; for example, for the KL criterion the accuracy differences are (+)0.74 at $\theta_0$, (+)0.46 at $\theta_{25}$, (-)0.03 at $\theta_{50}$, and (-)0.17 at $\theta_{75}$. 
Table 1

From the reported values, identify the main patterns the authors highlight: (i) rewinding subnetworks to the original initialization $\theta_0$ enables nearly all evaluated subnetworks (across the multiple pruning criteria) to become winning tickets (i.e., they satisfy $Accuracy(\mathcal{F}') + \xi \geq Accuracy(\mathcal{F})$ with small $\xi$), with the notable example of KL showing (+)0.74 at $\theta_0$; (ii) rewinding to later epochs (for instance $\theta_{50}$) often yields lower recovery accuracy across several criteria, consistent with the idea that subnetworks rewound later have less time to recover from structural damage. 
Table 1

Connect these empirical observations to prior literature and the authors' interpretation: the pattern that early rewinds (including $\theta_0$) outperform later rewinds aligns with prior observations that perturbations applied early are less damaging and that subnetworks discovered early are easier to recover, and the authors therefore conclude that resetting to $\theta_0$ or early epochs generally promotes layer-pruned subnetworks becoming winning tickets while rewinding to later epochs can reduce recovery accuracy. 
Achille et al. [2019]
You et al. [2020]

Start from the upstream result that weight rewinding to early epochs (including $\theta_0$) promotes layer-pruned subnetworks becoming winning tickets (i.e., the result established earlier that weight rewinding and early-epoch inheritance promote layer-pruned winning tickets is taken as given for this derivation).

Define the notion of "emergence early" used by the authors: a subnetwork is said to "emerge early" if the best-performing rewind epoch $\theta_i$ for that subnetwork occurs early in the dense network's training trajectory, indicating that the important parameters for recovery stabilize near the beginning of training.

Present the authors' empirical evidence that layer-pruned subnetworks emerge early: the rewind-experiment results in Table 1 show that for multiple pruning criteria the top-performing rewind epochs are early (for example, for expectABS the best result is at $\theta_0$; for KL the best is $\theta_0$ and the second best is $\theta_{25}$; other criteria similarly show best or top-two performance at early epochs), which the authors interpret as indicating that the important parameters of the subnetworks stabilize early and that the best-practice rewinding epochs for layer-pruned subnetworks are early in training. 
Table 1

Connect this observed early-emergence behavior to analogous findings in structured LTH and related literature: the authors cite prior works that draw early-bird tickets or find subnetworks early in training and argue that, analogous to filters-based structured LTH, layer-pruned subnetworks also exhibit early emergence, supporting practical rules for weight rewinding and early-bird detection when layers are the pruned structure. 
You et al. [2020]
Chen et al. [2022]

State the conclusion the authors draw: therefore, layer-pruned subnetworks share the structured-LTH property of emerging early, i.e., the best-practice rewinding epochs for layer-pruned subnetworks are early in the dense-network training trajectory, and this property holds across multiple pruning criteria according to the authors' experiments, informing practical rewinding and early-bird strategies for layer pruning.

open_questions.content: The authors acknowledge several unresolved scientific issues and limitations that remain after their findings. First, the presented initialization discovery strategy for layer-pruned winning tickets is one-shot (non-iterative) and therefore cannot be applied in its current form to iterative-pruning schemes that have been shown elsewhere to be more effective; developing an iterative, initialization-capable layer-pruning method is left open. Second, the layer-pruning LTH is theoretically and technically confined to residual-like architectures because identity shortcuts are essential to permit removal of layers without representation collapse; consequently the method is infeasible for plain (non-residual) networks such as VGG, and extending layer-pruning LTH to non-residual topologies is an open problem. Third, certain configurations of layer-pruned tickets underperform their dense counterparts (5 out of 14 reported cases) with no clear pattern; understanding the causes of these rare failures — for example interactions with depth, pruning location, dataset statistics, or optimization dynamics — is an unresolved issue. Fourth, out-of-distribution generalization exhibited inconsistent behavior across architectures (e.g., ResNet32 showed declines at higher pruning severity while ResNet56 improved); determining when and why layer-pruned initialization tickets generalize OOD remains to be investigated. Finally, a conceptual question is left open: to what extent does the choice of the eliminated structure (weights vs. filters vs. layers) fundamentally determine the emergence and properties of winning tickets and their recoverability at initialization? Answering these questions will require further theoretical analysis and broader empirical studies across architectures, datasets, pruning schedules and iterative schemes.
